capability_scale.1: Highest consequence or uncertainty: architecture, security, migration, recovery, release, and independent critical evaluation.
capability_scale.2: High-complexity bounded implementation against established contracts, with stronger review where hidden errors are consequential.
capability_scale.3: Bounded medium-complexity, reversible work with strong deterministic verification.
capability_scale.4: Wholly mechanical, low-consequence work with deterministic verification.

work_packages.rationale: The offline roster and evidence layout are bounded, reversible, and validator-backed, while C2 review protects against credential leakage or falsely qualifying an unavailable runtime.
This package fixes schema ownership, command authority, three-valued logic, and effect boundaries that every later package consumes, so both contract authorship and review require C1.

The synthetic-only monolith scaffold is reversible and deterministically checked by lockfile, build, dependency, startup, and credential-isolation tests, with C2 review for environment-boundary mistakes.
Authentication, bootstrap, step-up, RBAC, and ActorContext are substantial implementations from locked contracts, but a hidden bypass or first-user takeover requires independent C1 security review.
Identity normalization, merging, splitting, and endpoint rebinding are bounded domain implementation, yet errors could transfer permission or erase safety history and therefore demand C1 review.

Implementing consent, withdrawal, preference, suppression, and reconsent against approved semantics is C2 work, while any permissive mistake directly expands communication authority and needs C1 review.

The parameterized segment compiler is high-complexity implementation; UNKNOWN, negation, scope, or source-coverage defects can silently include recipients, so max effort and C1 logic/security review remain mandatory.
The journal adapter is a bounded implementation, but its acknowledgement, outage, replay, and restore barriers independently preserve denials and effect evidence, warranting max effort and C1 review.

Signed ingress and monotonic event reduction are complex but contract-bounded; invalid, duplicate, or out-of-order events could weaken restrictions, so C1 independently reviews negative and replay paths.
Provider and fake transports are high-complexity adapters, but acceptance-unknown classification, sender scope, suppression, and quota errors can duplicate or misdirect effects and require C1 review.

Renderer and codec work is complex but reversible and strongly verified by pinned revision, fallback, sanitization, and deterministic fixture tests, allowing only a one-step effort downshift with C2 review.

Atomic reservations, current eligibility, semantic deduplication, permits, retries, and unknown outcomes form the core effect executor; implementation is C2 under settled contracts with mandatory C1 concurrency/recovery review.

Forms, confirmation, and staged data movement are established C2 implementation, but replay, public identifiers, or mappings could invent permission, expose PII, or weaken denials and therefore need C1 review.
The manual CRUD workspace is bounded and reversible with server-scope, keyboard, screen-reader, and deterministic-focus oracles; C2 review covers scope presentation and accessibility consequences.

Campaign snapshots and lifecycle are complex bounded implementation, while partial resolution, stale approval, scheduling, cancellation, or uncertain completion defects can create unauthorized effects and require C1 review.

Proposal, revision, diff, and approval services implement settled exact-envelope semantics, but stale or self-approved consequential actions would expand authority, making max effort and C1 review necessary.

Instrumentation and rollups are high-complexity implementation because counters distinguish communications, interruptions, attempts, cost, weak evidence, and stale sources; C1 review guards operational and causal overclaims.
This package adjudicates real sender, renderer, security, restore, canary, and accountable-owner evidence before the first live release, so both evidence assembly and independent review require C1.

Although discovery is read-only, interpreting incomplete Kit topology, status classes, cursor evidence, legacy links, and cross-publication coupling defines later migration authority and needs C1 evidence reasoning and review.

The approved migration state machine is C2 implementation, but freezes, drains, checkpoints, authority epochs, negative reconciliation, and repair-forward rollback prevent dual sends and require C1 review.
Executing the first live authority transfer and judging canary, legacy opt-out, observation, and rollback evidence is irreversible and externally consequential, requiring C1 authorship and review.
A single durable executor is high-complexity C2 implementation, while cursor, wait/timeout, replay, cascade, and provider-acceptance races can lose or duplicate effects and mandate C1 review.
Sequences are bounded atop the shared runtime, but version pinning, reentry, withdrawal, reconsent, and migration-position errors can restart or rewrite recipient work and need C1 review.

Typed automations and their simulator are complex C2 implementation, while UNKNOWN conditions, waits, replay, loops, and actions could create permission shortcuts or unbounded effects and require C1 review.

Portfolio reuse and contextual preferences are C2 implementation, but cross-brand visibility, shared identity, fairness, and broader preference views could pool authority or leak relationships and demand C1 review.

Search, resumption, Inspect, and attention views are bounded reversible UX work with offline, stable-label, keyboard, and screen-reader verification; C2 review protects accessibility and authority legibility.

Goals, persistent preferences, and explicit session context are C2 implementation, while hidden memory, stale patches, or ambiguous workspace references could silently alter authoritative state and need C1 review.

The assistant is a bounded proposal layer, but context assembly, invalid model output, PII, cost, grants, safety blocks, and deterministic fallback cross security and authority boundaries requiring C1 review.

Delegation sessions are substantial implementation against explicit contracts, while attribution, scope, revocation, human-only approval, budget, and kill-switch failures could transfer authority and require C1 review.

The API and optional thin MCP are high-complexity exposure of existing commands, but discovery filtering, authentication, revision binding, idempotency, and approval parity are security boundaries needing C1 review.

Voice is complex integration over the textual assistant, while provisional transcription, ambiguity, microphone privacy, retention, cancellation, and mode handoff can create unintended authority or disclosure and need C1 review.

This is an adversarial qualification of computer use, stale state, restricted delegation, stop behavior, and human-only approval rather than routine UI implementation, so C1 must author and independently review the evidence.
Release qualification synthesizes red-team, privacy, vendor, accessibility, outage, operator, AI, agent, and voice evidence with a zero-invariant-breach condition, requiring C1 on both sides.
Each remaining live publication transfer requires fresh topology, cursor, legacy-negative, workflow, observation, owner, and rollback judgments, so repeated execution does not reduce it below C1.

Onsite placement is bounded C2 channel implementation, but personalization, tracking inference, shared devices, caching, expiration, and outage behavior can expose data or bypass consent and require C1 review.

A single qualified push use case is bounded C2 implementation, while endpoint secrets, device multiplicity, permission versus consent, withdrawal, quiet hours, and replacement behavior need C1 review.

Cross-channel routing is complex C2 implementation from approved semantics, but equivalence, pressure, preference, opt-out, complaints, unknown acceptance, and races could multiply or evade effects and require C1 review.

The evidence determines whether broader non-email activation is justified and must distinguish recipient value from extra volume while assessing pressure, accessibility, reliability, and incident ownership, requiring C1.

Choosing whether a phone or app channel is feasible joins actual demand, market law, provider rules, consent, replies, geography, cost, and product-scope constraints, so C1 authorship and review are necessary.

Runbooks and deployment machinery are high-complexity implementation, while secrets, migrations, journal access, rollback, restore, and an independent send fence have production safety consequences requiring C1 review.

Independent attacker-boundary review integrates authorization, rendering, ingress, dependencies, and external effects and can hold the release for critical findings, so the review package itself remains C1 with C1 verification.

Restore and failure qualification must reason across PITR, independent journal replay, post-backup denials, accepted-before-crash uncertainty, RPO/RTO, and load isolation, demanding C1 authorship and review.

The mature-profile release decision reconciles exact artifact identity, applicable must-pass evidence, optional-profile boundaries, owner sign-off, maintenance, incidents, and outstanding brand gates, requiring C1 throughout.

Measured replacement of provider, queue, analytics, cache, workflow, or service boundaries is an architectural cost/reliability decision that must preserve authority and recovery semantics, so it remains C1 despite a high risk label.
